title: No compulsion, still
tomorrow: a friend's question turns into an argument. stay or walk away?

segments.voice: Yesterday, answering questions with two honest words: I don't know. A limit on what you claim. Today, a limit on how hard you push what you do know.
screen: `I DON'T KNOW.` → `NOW: HOW HARD DO YOU PUSH?`

segments.voice: Somebody discovers a podcast, a diet, a running app, and suddenly every conversation bends toward it. Friends start answering their texts a little slower. So when someone is curious about what you love, how much do you share? The Qur'an's answer sits in a strange spot. Just before it comes the passage known as the Throne Verse: a God who never tires and never sleeps, whose throne takes in the heavens and the earth. Power, as big as the book describes it. And the very next line says: "There is no compulsion in religion." Why put that there?
screen: `EVERY CONVERSATION BENDS.` → `THE THRONE VERSE.` → `THEN: NO COMPULSION.`

segments.voice: Read on and the puzzle starts to solve itself. In Pickthall's words: "The right direction is henceforth distinct from error." The case has been made, clearly. Power that big doesn't need a headlock; the choice is left with the person. A report in Sunan Abu Dawud gives the verse a human setting. Some families in Medina had children who had grown up among a Jewish tribe of the city, and when that tribe had to leave Medina, the parents said they would not let their children go. The verse came: no compulsion in religion. Not even, the report suggests, for your own child. The Qur'an says the same to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ himself: he is there to remind, it says, not to stand guard over anyone. And it gives the method: "Call unto the way of thy Lord with wisdom and fair exhortation, and reason with them in the better way." So sharing is welcome: wisdom, beauty, a good reason, offered when someone's asking. What it can't become is pressure. The tenth link. The guilt trip. The friendship that only exists for the pitch. One for tonight: the Qur'an's line against forcing anyone sits right after its picture of God holding up the heavens.
screen: `THE RIGHT WAY IS CLEAR.` · `NOT EVEN YOUR OWN CHILD.` · `A REMINDER, NOT A GUARD.` · `WISDOM AND FAIR EXHORTATION.` · then, large: `SHARE, DON'T PUSH.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands open on your knees, palms up: something held out, nothing gripped. Keep them open for the whole sit. If someone you'd love to share your faith with comes to mind, keep the hands open toward them too.
No compulsion: belief can't be forced, so sharing stays an offer. From 2:256, right after the Throne Verse.
Hold onto this: share, don't push, with the hand left open. Seven of ten, offered.

screen: `DAY 1752 COUNTS.` → `TEACHING AND PASSING IT ON · 7 OF 10.` → `TOMORROW: A QUESTION TURNS INTO AN ARGUMENT. STAY OR GO?`

howItsDone: Muslims share their faith through what the Qur'an calls wisdom and fair exhortation: answering when asked, inviting friends to an iftar or an open mosque day, and leaving the choice with the listener.

fork.setup: at a party, a classmate asks why you're not drinking. you have a whole speech ready about it. what fits 'share, don't push'?
options: give the full speech. she asked, so she wants all of it.
give one short, honest reason, and let her ask more if she wants.
dodge with 'i'm driving'. faith is private, so keep it out.
fork.reveal: the Qur'an's method is wisdom and fair exhortation, and 2:256 leaves the choice with the listener. a short true answer is an offer; the speech turns into a push, and the dodge shares nothing.

sources.quoted: There is no compulsion in religion. The right direction is henceforth distinct from error.
Call unto the way of thy Lord with wisdom and fair exhortation, and reason with them in the better way.

notes: Abu Dawud 2682 (Ibn 'Abbas): children of Ansar families raised among the Banu Nadir; when the tribe was expelled, the parents said 'we will not leave our children'; 2:256 came. Told gently ('had to leave Medina'; the tribe is not named in the voice). Confirm numbering, grading and that 'not even your own child' is a fair reading.

2:255 paraphrased (never tires, never sleeps, throne takes in the heavens and the earth); 88:21–22 paraphrased. Title says 'still': an earlier lesson on 2:256 exists; this one takes the placement puzzle and the Abu Dawud setting as its angle.
